root.note: Italian banca comes from a Germanic word for ‘bench’ (Lombard or Old High German); dictionaries differ on which Germanic language was the source.

history: A bank was first a piece of furniture. Germanic peoples who settled in Italy, such as the Lombards, used a word for ‘bench’, and Italian took it as banca. In the medieval cities of Tuscany and Lombardy, money-changers did their business at benches in the street. The bench gave its name to the trade and then to the institution. When a banker failed, his bench was supposedly broken, and that is the picture behind Italian bancarotta, from banca rotta, ‘broken bench’, and English bankrupt. The English words bank and bench are cousins. Italian also has banco, a counter, a school desk or a market stall, and in a post office or bank you will see sportello for the window.
historyEinfach: Banca comes from a Germanic word for ‘bench’. In medieval Italian cities money-changers worked at benches. The word for the bench became the word for the bank. Bancarotta means ‘broken bench’, that is, bankruptcy.

elsewhere.text: The Italian phrase went through French into English, where it was reshaped to look like a Latin participle.
